14 THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE

be a teacher and of his purpose and aim in establishing a school:

When the war closed, the cause for which he had fought was lost, and he was left penniless and without resources. Looking about him for a means of livelihood, he began to seek a new field of service. Looking about him, he bethought himself of teaching, the children of those with whom he had fought; but now that the clash of arms was over, he began to seek a new field of service. Looking about him he remembered the children of those he had loved, and with whom he had fought, with swords and bayonets and armed himself, he could not find the standard of education, to prepare them for the world, his means were in the grander, holier work of truth." By means, he settled in that little village, not yet known as Savoy, to begin the struggle for an education—to arm his boys for the conflict of life.

He practiced the most rigid principles of economy, both with his own people and the saving of others. A man both with the gifts of the more popular type, in the opinion of the gentler of the quieter type, and the more reserved was Professor Holland was the younger, was accorded the most careful treatment and consideration. Professor Holland was venerable and successful instructor. [Sam Doak Terry?]

W. A. Carter, writing in the same year (1886), offers the information that Savoy College was not confined to Texas when he was teaching; and in Texas he received his education in the Lawyers' Institute of Ladonia, in Fannin County. "Being a thorough scholar," he was not unknown in the county.²¹

²¹Carter, W. A., op. cit., p. 95.
²²Interview with Mr. Morrison, conducted at Savoy, Texas, August 7, 1938.
